cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
We have learned how currents produce magnetic fields.
Now let's ask what a magnetic field does to a moving charge.
The magnetic force is q times velocity cross magnetic field.
Its magnitude is the absolute value of charge times speed times field strength
times sine of the angle between velocity and field.
That angle belongs between velocity and B, not between force and B.
Imagine a positive charge moving right while the field points into the page,
shown by crosses.
Right cross into the page gives upward force.
For a negative charge moving the same way, reverse that answer: the force is
downward.
Take a moment to picture both arrows.
Your right hand rule finds velocity cross B first; the sign of charge comes
afterward.
A stationary particle has no magnetic force.
A particle moving parallel or opposite to the field also has zero magnetic
force, because the sine is zero.
Perpendicular motion gives the largest magnitude.
For charge two microcoulombs, speed three hundred meters per second, and
perpendicular field zero point five tesla, the force is three times ten to the
minus four newtons.
If the angle becomes thirty degrees, the force halves.
In JEE questions, settle the direction and angle before doing arithmetic.
The cross product is more than a formula: it tells us which way the path
starts
to bend.
Can a magnetic field make a particle faster?
With magnetic force alone, no.
Force is always perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity.
Power is force dot velocity, which is zero.
So magnetic work is zero and kinetic energy stays constant.
Velocity can still change, because velocity includes direction.
Think of steering a moving bicycle without increasing its speed: changing
direction is a real acceleration.
Our particle is an idealized example, with no electric field, gravity or
collisions affecting the motion, and radiation neglected.
We also use speeds small compared with the speed of light.
In a uniform magnetic field, if velocity is initially perpendicular to B, the
force stays perpendicular to velocity and has constant magnitude.
It acts as the centripetal force for a circular path.
Set absolute q times v times B equal to m times v squared divided by r.
Cancel one v, and the radius is m v divided by absolute q B.
Larger momentum means a wider circle.
Stronger field or larger charge magnitude means a tighter circle.
A negative charge bends the opposite way but has the same radius as a positive
particle with the same mass, speed and charge magnitude.
Do not confuse no work with no acceleration.
Speed stays fixed, while the direction keeps turning.
And do not use the circle formula for every magnetic field: a nonuniform field
can produce a more complicated trajectory.
Let's give the circle some numbers.
A proton enters a uniform field of zero point two zero tesla at one million
meters per second, perpendicular to the field.
Use proton mass one point six seven times ten to the minus twenty seven
kilograms and charge magnitude one point six zero times ten to the minus
nineteen coulombs.
Radius is mass times speed divided by charge magnitude times field.
The result is about zero point zero five two two meters, or five point two two
centimeters.
Now how long does one turn take?
Time equals circumference divided by speed: two pi r over v.
Substituting the radius cancels v and gives period two pi m over absolute q B.
For this proton, the period is about zero point three two eight microseconds.
Double its speed within our nonrelativistic model.
What changes?
Pause and decide.
The radius doubles, but the period stays the same: the longer circumference is
traveled at twice the speed.
For a semicircular passage through a suitable field region, travel time is
half
the period.
The distance traveled is pi r, while displacement magnitude between the
endpoints is two r.
Those are different quantities.
Here the endpoint separation is about ten point four four centimeters.
Always check the region's geometry before assuming the particle actually
completes a semicircle.
A boundary can make it leave earlier, and the direction of charge decides
which
side it bends toward.
What if the velocity is neither parallel nor perpendicular to the field?
Split it into two components.
The parallel component is v cosine theta, and the perpendicular component is v
sine theta, with theta measured from the magnetic field direction.
The parallel component produces no magnetic force and stays constant.
The perpendicular component rotates exactly as in circular motion.
Combine that circle with steady progress along the field, and the path becomes
a helix.
Its radius uses only perpendicular speed: m v perpendicular divided by
absolute q B.
Its period remains two pi m divided by absolute q B.
The pitch is axial displacement during one turn, so multiply parallel velocity
by the period.
Using our same proton and field, let total speed be one million meters per
second at thirty degrees to B.
Perpendicular speed is half a million meters per second, and parallel speed is
about eight hundred sixty six thousand meters per second.
The radius becomes two point six one centimeters.
The period stays about zero point three two eight microseconds, and pitch is
about zero point two eight four meters.
At ninety degrees, parallel speed vanishes, so the helix becomes a circle with
zero pitch.
At zero degrees, perpendicular speed vanishes and the particle moves straight
along B; there is no actual circular orbit to time.
A negative charge reverses the rotational sense, not the unchanged parallel
motion.
Keep those two independent pieces separate in your sketch.
Finally, bring in an electric field.
The total electromagnetic force is q times the quantity E plus velocity cross
B.
Unlike magnetic force, electric force can have a component along motion and
can
change kinetic energy.
A velocity selector uses perpendicular electric and magnetic fields to let one
speed pass without deflection.
Picture velocity to the right and magnetic field into the page.
For a positive charge, magnetic force points upward.
Choose the electric field downward, so electric force points downward.
At the selected speed, the magnitudes match: absolute q E equals absolute q
v B.
Cancel the charge magnitude and get v equal to E divided by B.
Take electric field six thousand newtons per coulomb and magnetic field zero
point zero two tesla.
Selected speed is three hundred thousand meters per second.
For negative charges, both forces reverse, so cancellation still occurs at the
same speed when the entry direction is unchanged.
A faster positive particle initially bends upward, because its magnetic force
is larger.
A slower positive particle initially bends downward.
Equal magnitudes would not cancel if the force directions were the same, so
draw the vectors first.
This is a crossed field application, not a claim that all electric and
magnetic
motion is circular.
Our toolkit now has force direction, unchanged speed under magnetic force
alone, circle radius and period, helical pitch, and a selector condition.
Try the practice questions, keeping the physical assumptions beside each
formula.
